9 1.10.11 Composition of the Board and Quorum Requirements.
The Board of Education is to consist of seventeen (17) public members appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Rhode Island Senate.
The Chair of the Governor's Workforce Board, or designee, and the Chair of the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation, or designee, shall serve as non-­‐voting, ex-­‐officio members of the board.
The Governor shall select from the appointed members a chairperson and vice chairperson.
A quorum shall consist of nine (9) members of the board.
A majority vote of those present shall be required for action.
The Chair of the Board shall have no term and shall serve at the pleasure of the governor. 1.10.12 Chief Responsibility of the Board.
According to its webpage (http://www.ride.ri.gov/BoardofEducation/BoardMembers.aspx, accessed 1/5/17), “The Board of Education is the chief policy-­‐setting body overseeing K-­‐20 education in Rhode Island.
Through its designated powers and duties, the Board helps shape the course of public education to ensure that all of the state's students receive the best possible education.” Council on Postsecondary Education 1.20.10 Background.

In June of 2014, the Board of Education voted to establish two separate sub-­‐councils, one being the Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, the other being the Council on Postsecondary Education.
The Council on Postsecondary Education is chiefly in charge of those matters relating to the University of Rhode Island for which university-­‐internal approval is not sufficient. “The Council is an independent public corporation vested with the responsibility of providing oversight for the system of public higher education in Rhode Island.
This system consists of three public institutions of higher learning, the University of Rhode Island (URI), Rhode Island College (RIC), and the Community College of Rhode Island (CCRI), along with the Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner.
The Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner, which operates under the direction of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, is the administrative and research arm of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.” (https://www.riopc.edu/page/Council%20overview/) 1.20.11 Composition of the Council.

The Council on Postsecondary Education comprises eight members appointed by the Governor from the members of the Board of Education, to serve until their terms on the Board expire, and one non-­‐voting student member appointed for a two-­‐year term from one of the three public Rhode Island institutions of higher learning.
The Council’s chair shall be appointed by the Governor from one of the eight voting members of the Council.
In addition, the Chair of the Board of Education shall serve on the Council in an ex officio, non-­‐voting capacity. (see RIGL §16-­‐59-­‐2). 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Council.
The Council’s responsibilities include (for more details, see Rhode Island General laws § 16-­‐59-­‐1 and § 16-­‐59-­‐4): (1) It shall retain all authority formerly vested in the Board of Education regarding the employment

10 of faculty and staff at the public higher education institutions. (2) It shall prepare and maintain a five (5) year funding plan for higher education that implements the strategic financing recommendations of the Board of Education. (3) It shall prepare with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education and to present annually to the State Budget Officer in accordance with § 35-­‐3-­‐4 a state higher education budget.

Prior to submitting the budget to the State Budget Officer as required by the budget office instructions and this subsection, the Council shall present the budget to the Board of Education for its review and approval. (4) It shall appoint and dismiss presidents of the public institutions of higher learning with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, and to establish procedures for this, and with the assistance of the Commissioner to approve or disapprove vice presidents of the public institutions of higher learning appointed by the respective presidents of the public institutions of higher learning. (5) It shall delegate to the presidents of each public higher education institution the authority and responsibility for operational and management decisions related to their institutions, consistent with the goals of the statewide strategic plan for postsecondary education, provided however that the presidents may be required to provide information or updates to the council regarding any delegated operational or management decisions.
The President of the University 1.30.10 Presidential Powers—Shared Governance.

In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-­‐ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).
The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary education pursuant to § 16-­‐59-­‐4” (See RI General Law § 16-­‐32-­‐2.1).

The law stipulates, however, that this authority is to be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with § 16-­‐32-­‐10,” which states that it “shall also be the duty of the president and a committee of the faculty, . . . to arrange courses of study conforming to all acts of Congress, and prescribe any qualifications for the admission of students and any rules of study, exercise, discipline, and government as the president and committee may deem proper.” For more than half a century, the committee of the faculty mentioned in this legislation has been understood to be the URI Faculty Senate.

University Manual Chapter 7 Faculty and Staff 7.11.11 Full-­‐time non tenure-­‐track teaching positions.
The three titles of full-­‐time non tenure-­‐track teaching positions include Lecturer, Senior Lecturer, and Teaching Professor.

The Lecturer title is used to designate appointments of persons who are serving in a teaching capacity for a defined period of time.
There are two types of lecturers: Lecturer is defined as a position in which an individual may be appointed to multiple one-­‐year appointments.
Lecturers may be eligible for the promotional process to Senior Lecturer.
For more details, including, for example, degree requirements, annual review cycles, expectations and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP.
Temporary Lecturer is temporarily employed to cover courses for full-­‐time faculty who are on sabbatical leaves, sick leaves, or in some cases in the interval between the allocation of a new faculty position and the subsequent appointment of the new faculty.
Temporary lecturers shall not be eligible for the promotional process to Senior Lecturer or Teaching Professor.
For more details, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP.

Senior Lecturer: promotion to Senior Lecturer shall follow an evaluation/review of teaching effectiveness and student advising within the college at the end of the 4th year for promotion in the 5th year.
The promotional procedure shall be evidence based.
Appointments shall be based upon excellence in teaching and advising starting in the fifth (5th) year and shall be for periods of two years with possible reappointments of

12 two (2) years duration.
Those Senior Lecturers without a terminal degree after three 2-­‐ year reappointments may be granted renewable three year appointments.
For more details, including, for example, degree requirements, annual review cycles, expectations and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP.
Teaching Professor: promotion to Teaching Professor shall require a terminal degree in the appropriate discipline and shall follow a comprehensive review in the 8th year with demonstrated excellence in teaching effectiveness and student advising.
In the ninth (9th) year, a Senior Lecturer, who has shown excellence in teaching and advising, and has been on continuous appointments as a Lecturer and Senior Lecturer, may be recommended to the Provost by the Chair and/or Dean to become a Teaching Professor with an initial four (4) year contract and possible four (4) year reappointments.
For more details, including, for example, annual review cycles, expectations and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP.

Lecturers shall be expected to participate in department service activities pertaining to their normal instructional responsibilities.
Senior Lecturers and Teaching Professors are expected to perform college and university service.
For more details on full-­‐time, non-­‐ tenure-­‐track teaching positions, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP. 7.11.25 Non tenure-­‐track Clinical Professor shall be appointed in the College of Pharmacy, the College of Nursing, and other colleges and departments requiring clinical training to contribute to the instruction, practice scholarship, supervision, and service in a clinical setting.
Non tenure-­‐track clinical faculty will have salaried appointments of more than 20 hours per week (greater than 50% FTE) that exceed or are expected to exceed one year in duration and are supported wholly or in part by general revenue funds.
Non tenure-­‐track clinical faculty shall not be eligible for tenure or permanent status.
There are three Clinical Faculty ranks, Clinical Assistant Professor (see 7.11.25a), Clinical Associate Professor (see 7.11.25b), and Clinical Professor (see 7.11.25c).

For more details on non tenure track Clinical Faculty, including, for example, annual review cycles and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP. 7.11.25a Clinical Assistant Professor shall hold a terminal professional degree in the clinical field with training and experience in an area of clinical specialization.
There must be clear evidence of a high level of ability in clinical practice, training and teaching.
Initial appointments for Clinical Assistant Professor positions shall be for two years with possible extension following a review.
The second appointment cycle shall be for a period of 3 years with possible 3-­‐year extensions. 7.11.25b Clinical Associate Professor.
In addition to the qualifications required of a Clinical Assistant Professor, the appointee shall have had extensive successful experience in clinical practice in a field of specialization and in working with and/or

13 directing others (such as professionals, faculty members, graduate students, fellows, and residents or interns) in clinical activities in the field.
The appointee must also have demonstrated superior clinical practice and teaching ability and accomplishments.
Appointments for Clinical Associate Professor positions shall be for three years with possible reappointments. 7.11.25c Clinical Professor.
In addition to the qualifications required of a Clinical Associate Professor, the appointee shall have demonstrated a degree of excellence in clinical practice and teaching sufficient to establish an excellent regional and national reputation among colleagues.
The appointee shall also have demonstrated extraordinary professional competence and leadership.
Appointments for Clinical Professors shall be for four years with possible reappointments. 7.11.29 Non tenure-­‐track Research Faculty are employed to contribute to the research mission of the institution, have salaried appointments of more than 20 hours per week (greater than 50% FTE) that exceed or are expected to exceed one year in duration, and are supported by non-­‐general revenue funds.

Non-­‐tenure-­‐track research faculty shall not be eligible for tenure or permanent status.
There are three Research Faculty ranks: Assistant Research Professor (see 7.11.29a), Associate Research Professor (see 7.11.29b), and Research Professor (see 7.11.29c).
For more details on non tenure-­‐track Research Faculty, including annual review cycles and promotion information, see the Agreement between the RI Council of Postsecondary Education and the URI Chapter of the AAUP. 7.11.29a Assistant Research Professors shall have demonstrated research ability and potential for contributing to the research, scholarly, or creative mission of the institution.
Appointees should be qualified and competent to direct the work of others (such as technicians, graduate students, other research personnel).
An earned doctoral degree shall be a requirement for appointment at this rank.
Appointment to this non tenure-­‐ track faculty rank is dependent on extramural funding that supports the salary and fringe benefits of the individual, as well as excellence in performance. 7.11.29b Associate Research Professor.

In addition to the qualifications required of the Assistant Research Professor, appointees shall have extensive successful experience in research, scholarly or creative endeavors, and the demonstrated ability to propose, develop, and manage major research projects.
Appointment to this non tenure-­‐track faculty rank is dependent on extramural funding that supports the salary and fringe benefits of the individual and excellence in performance. 7.11.29c Research Professor.
In addition to the qualifications required of the Associate Research Professor, appointees shall have demonstrated superior accomplishments to establish an excellent reputation among national or international colleagues.
Appointees should have a record of outstanding scholarly production in research, publications, professional achievements or exhibit excellence in research leadership.
Appointment to this non tenure-­‐track faculty rank is dependent on extramural funding that supports the salary and fringe benefits of the individual and excellence in performance.

14 7.11.30 Non tenure-­‐track Faculty of Practice will have salaried appointments of more than 20 hours a week (greater than 50% FTE) that exceed or are expected to exceed one year in duration and are supported wholly or in part by general revenue funds. They shall not be tenured and are not eligible for permanent status. Their primary duties and responsibilities shall be teaching. Appointments to Faculty of Practice positions are reserved for accomplished or distinguished individuals who have demonstrated skills and expertise acquired in their chosen field of practice. Examples include, but are not limited to, leaders in business, engineering, science, theatre, dance, music, and art. Appointees to the position of Faculty of Practice shall hold professional masters degrees or terminal degrees in their field or shall show evidence of equivalent capabilities by virtue of experience. Faculty of Practice shall be appointed after being vetted with the department and with approval of the Dean. Appointment to the position of Faculty of Practice shall be on an annual basis for a period of up to five years maximum. PROPOSAL: THE HONORS INSTITUTE Organizational Change – Creation of Honors Institute and Addition to Chapter 3 The Honors Program proposes expanding its scope and consolidating its operations under a new aegis, the Honors Institute.
The new institute contains the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – entities that already fall ad hoc under the umbrella of “Honors.” The creation of the Honors Institute will require organizational change.
It will reside in Chapter 3 of the University Manual.
The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be responsible for its oversight and report to the Provost.
The Executive Director and Assistant Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be the Director and Assistant Director of the Honors Program.
An Advisory Council will be appointed by the Executive Director of the Honors Institute to include faculty representatives from Colleges across the University, Honors student leadership, and major external stakeholders.

The Honors Institute will not figure in Chapter 8 under “Centers and Institutes” (8.90.10-8.90.40) since the Honors Institute, an academic institute, is not the type of institute that this section was intended to govern.
The Honors Program is only one entity housed under the umbrella structure of the Honors Institute.
University Manual language [8.60.10-8.65.12] remains unchanged, including: ● Program Direction and Development.
The Director of the Honors Program in collaboration with the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee shall be responsible for overseeing the Honors Program (8.64.10) ● “The Teaching, Advisement and Assessment Committee shall conduct periodic evaluations of the Honors Program and its separate components” [8.64.12].
Rationale for the creation of an Honors Institute In its current form, “Honors” at URI is minimally competitive with Honors education at our peer flagship institutions.

First, Honors education at URI largely does not meet national best practices and standards in terms of curriculum. (The Honors Program directors will be submitting a redesigned curriculum to the Faculty Senate soon.) Second, and more important to this proposal: The “Honors” ecosystem – the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – is minimally integrated into the larger University, which has resulted in a lack of visibility and support.
In their “External Review Report” in 2023, National Collegiate Honors Council reviewers recognized that a transformation into an honors college was not feasible due to financial constraints at URI.
To compete with honors colleges all around us, and to house a 21st-century Honors Program, they recommended establishing an Honors Institute that pulls together officially the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities.
This highly visible and fully integrated entity would operate on par with the colleges and thus enhance operational efficiency.

The reviewers stated that the creation of a formal Honors Institute will “result in significant long-term returns to the University by raising its academic profile, by attracting a portion of the large number of high-achieving students who are available in the wider area but do not choose to attend URI, and by increasing the amount of annual giving to URI.” Further still, the external reviewers affirm that the success of an Honors Institute “could have ripple effects that launch the University of Rhode Island toward the highest tier of institutions in the Northeast.” Budget The Honors Institute will keep its existing budget infrastructure.
This includes a Fund 100 base budget and external Foundation funding.
The current internal funding is sufficient for the Institute’s operations.
In the shift to an IBB model, Honors will be classified as a central service; we anticipate no decrease in levels of funding to Honors operations.

University Manual language for Chapter 3 3.60.10 The Honors Institute contains the Honors Program (see 8.60.10 - 8.65.12) and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities. 3.60.11 The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall report to the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs, and shall have primary responsibility for administering the policies and procedures of this administrative unit. 3.60.12 The Executive Director shall be a non-voting ex officio member of the Honors Program Curriculum and Advisory Committee. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: Department of Journalism & Public Relations, see Appendix A This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is cur rently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department.

V. 23.09.29 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Non-Standard form for curricular changes Only to be used in cases not appropriate for Kuali A Proposal to Fully Integrate the Public Relations Program into the Department of Journalism, Creating a New Department of Journalism and Public Relations Date: 10/27/23 Proposer Name: Professor Norbert Mundorf Department: Communication Studies 1.
Describe the change you are proposing.
This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is currently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department. 2.
Give the rationale for your proposed change.
In 1997, the B.A. in Public Relations was approved as an interdepartmental program jointly run by the Communication Studies department and the Journalism department.

The original legislation (Bill #96- 97-26) called for the program to be administered on a “three-year rotating basis by the Chairs of Journalism and Communication Studies” with an “advisory/admissions committee” comprised of both chairs from the respective departments and the faculty who taught in the program.
Somewhere in the twenty-five plus years that have elapsed since the original proposal, the Public Relations program was effectively subsumed by Communication Studies and the interdepartmental structure of the original vision was lost.
During the academic program review of Journalism this past year, external reviewers suggested the Journalism curriculum would benefit from a “rethinking of [Harrington’s] overall department structure.” While it was originally proposed that the department might merge with the program in Sports Media Communication, subsequent conversations with faculty suggested that public relations would be a better fit as this pairing is common in institutions across the country and presents additional opportunities for collaboration due to the curricular overlap between the two programs.
Interestingly, the original proposal to create the public relations program also emphasized the importance of this relationship: “Because the existing Public Relations courses are Journalism courses,

V. 23.09.29 because the existing minor has been administered by the chair of Journalism, and because of the extent of the chair’s involvement in the existing internship program, the chair of Journalism will serve as the initial administrator of the program.” Following the guidance of the reviewers and in the spirit of the original vision for this program, the proposed organizational change will restore the interdisciplinary vision for the Public Relations program. It will allow for resource sharing and interdisciplinary collaboration between programs and will also help to rectify a primary issue addressed in the Journalism academic program review, namely, the absence of a Chair. In order to address this leadership gap and ensure a successful start to this new department, a search for a Full Professor who will Chair this new department is currently underway. 3. List all programs/courses/departments/schools, etc. that this change affects. This change will affect the Public Relations BA program (currently housed in Communication Studies department) and Journalism BA program and Journalism department. These units are housed in the Harrington School of Communication and Media in the College of Arts and Sciences. 4. Include any necessary letters of support. Letters of support are included from the faculty of the public relations program , the department of Journalism, the Director of the Harrington School of Communication and Media, and the Dean of Arts and Sciences. Signature: __________________________________________________ Date:___10-31-2023_____ Please send completed form and all necessary supporting documents to Faculty Senate Specialist Genviéve Spitale via email: genvieve.spitale@uri.edu

The University of Rhode Island is an equal opportunity employer committed to community, equity, and diversity and to the principles of affirmative action. 29 October 2023 Support for new Department of Journalism and Public Relations As Dean of Arts and Sciences, I fully support the proposed integration of Public Relations with the Journalism Department to create a new Department of Journalism and Public Relations. This merger does not impact the academic programs in any way. Nationally, many institutions have journalism and public relations programs in the same department. Students and faculty both benefit from the synergies between the two disciplines. The merger will also enable more effective use of resources, while also freeing the Department of Communication Studies to focus more fully on their major, as well as continue to provide a home for the rapidly expanding sports communication and media major. FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 NOVEMBER 7, 2024 Dear Senators, Our community at-large and the faculty senate are both committed to protecting expressive speech as a core right underpinning academic freedom at the University of Rhode Island.
The recent DRAFT University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property, if approved without revision, would undermine this right.
It girds an overly vague set of conditions for the use of property with punitive consequences to be administered with vague guidelines and unfettered power.
Despite the inclusion of language which emphasizes learning, the letter makes no specific reference to academic freedom or its prominence in our University Manual (Chapter 6).
In this letter, I summarize the phases of the regulation's evolution over the past several months, as far as I am aware.
Then, I provide a short summary of the major concerns about the regulation that senators and other community members have identified.
Finally, I outline next steps.

Timeline • Spring/Summer 2024: Various communications from the URI administration indicated that lack of a policy pertaining to protest and its potential harms, particularly with respect to university property, was a concern. • Late August 2024: In writing, I requested senate review of policy drafts given potential bearing on academic life.
I received no reply in advance of the below steps. • Early October 2024: The DRAFT regulations were presented to the Administrative Policy Committee (on which I sit as Senate President) by Vice President of Administration and Finance (VPAF) Benson.
The DRAFT regulation was supplied one hour.
I raised concerns about austerity and potential impacts at the meeting, despite having to comment in real-time.
It was posted for public comment by the next day. • Mid-October 2024: Concerns arise in the community following communications to union members by the AAUP-URI executive director. • Late October 2024: Senate leadership meets with the VPAF and her staff.
The parties tentatively agree to participate in an ad hoc committee to assist with redress of the substantive problems, in addition to holding a forum at the next senate meeting.

Process issues about how these policies were shared and not properly vetted will be addressed at a future time.
Major Concerns Many senators have written to me by email or posted comments (400+) to the VPAFs policy site.
Of these, I am attaching four letters from senators and faculty, as well as a comment

written by the Rhode Island ACLU Executive Director and sent to the VPAF on the matter.
At a minimum, the following major areas of concern have been cited as areas of major concern around the proposed regulation. • The need for a policy or regulation to react to protest events on a campus that has essentially never seen violent protest, and which has a tradition of peaceful, participatory, and deliberative discourse, is ostensibly undocumented. • The policy is very vague on how response to property damage events will be pursued.
References to other handbooks, manuals, contracts, and laws seem to have been sufficient to manage any event involving damage to property in the past.

It is not clear how these policies will be enacted differently under this regulation, or if they should be. • Even if the regulation is stood up, there is a seemingly draconian presentation of severe punishments bereft of clear attendant policy, due process, and collective participation of appropriate university bodies. • There is a clear lack of common sense considerations in the regulation, such as faculty not being able to access their labs in off-hours, punishments for simple infractions such as littering with a flyer, and so on. • The forceful, top-down style, in the document and in procedural choices, contrasts starkly with the norms of a community that prides itself on academic freedom, constructive expressive speech, and civility, and with the expectations of a senate that is an equal partner in shared governance.
Charge to Attend and Engage Modern universities should form an intellectually safe, free marketplace of ideas.
Our faculty and students need to be able to express themselves without the weight of oppressive and potentially life altering consequences hanging over their heads while engaging in study, life and work.

This is especially true for our students who are learning to use their voices for change and good.
This DRAFT regulation is clearly not in-line with these imperatives.
Our task is to ensure that these issues are addressed through our deliberations and advocacy, and, if necessary, through legislation.
Please join us at the next Faculty Senate meeting on November 14 at 3:00 PM in the Hope Room, Higgins Welcome Center, at which time this matter will be discussed.
There are other important topics on the agenda, and many people will wish to speak on this matter, so please come prepared with concise statements.
We will not be addressing matters of university and senate process around policies and regulations at this meeting; however, we will be considering this need at another time.
Sincerely, Theodore (Ted) Walls URI Faculty Senate President, 2024-2025

Senator Koray Ozpolat 10/15/2024 Comments on the proposed regulations regarding the use of university property In principle, I agree that the university may establish reasonable standards and limitations regarding time, place and manner of use for university property.
Most of the listed limitations and prohibited activities (2a-2o) look reasonable.
However, I have three concerns (i) 2g. signs, posting and banners (ii) 3.
Enforcements and Violations, (iii) the timing of this proposal Motivation “Academic institutions exist for the transmission of knowledge, the pursuit of truth, the development of students, and the general well-being of society.
Free inquiry and free expression are indispensable to the attainment of these goals. “(AAUP Joint Statement) I believe it is important that URI remains an open space for students, faculty, and staff to exchange ideas and express themselves.
While protecting the university property matters, our strategic goal is to develop young minds to think critically and globally.

That’s how we can develop the leaders of the future who will “commit to addressing the most pressing issues facing our state and the global community” as mentioned in URI’s Strategic Priority-1 Concerns I am worried that with “somewhat” restrictive property policies and harsh sanctions for violations, the proposed regulations may broadly discourage students and faculty from engaging in campus activism, protests and demonstrations.
For example, if a student affixes a poster or a sign to the exterior of a building, could s/he face disciplinary action up to termination?
I would say “let them post” and URI employees can pull unauthorized posters later.
Why punish our students?
I am concerned about the timing of this proposal too.
What events put this proposal forward?
To the best of my knowledge, we did not have any encampments, or damage to campus property this year.
Is our administration under pressure from donors or politicians?
Conclusion After 13 years at URI, it is clear to me that political violence or destruction of campus property are not big issues in Kingston but on the contrary, it is lack of dissent and weak activism that slows down the growth of our students.

Many URI students have no idea or don’t care about what is going on beyond their small worlds!
Any policy that directly/indirectly discourages (the already weak) campus activism and demonstrations actually hurts the development of our students and I propose that • 2g is removed • The disciplinary actions for other violations be clarified • URI Administration shares with us - why now, justify the need for these restrictions • The introduction paragraph of the document can be extended to underline freedom of speech & assembly as vital elements of academic freedom and that buildings partially serve this purpose.

Thoughts on draft regulations for use of URI property: The draft is very legalistic and very top-down; it is “command-and-control” in tone.
The subtext of the regulations is that misbehavior will not be tolerated.
I’m not sure that is an eCective message to control the members of a University community.
The Introduction does not mention the special role of the University as a place where dissent is protected, and where the interruption of normal activities by peaceful civil disobedience is accepted for its potential contribution to civic discourse and social change.
As a place that honors free speech, the University should project collegiality and respect, even in laying down rules.
Some prohibitions in the draft are unnecessarily granular, treating such things as discarded leaﬂets (litter), impeding traCic, hanging banners, etc., which might occur during demonstrations, as punishable oCences.
History shows that prohibition of minor and incidental acts is often an invitation to law-breaking and/or an excuse to arrest, rather than an eCective way of controlling behavior.

It should also be noted that such prohibitions foster cynicism and undermine the trust of community members in their leaders and their pride in representing the institution.
The option of achieving community peace through consultation and dialogue with parties in conﬂict is not mentioned.
However, this is a far more eCective way to achieve the apparent goals of the draft, without threats and without talking down to the University community.
I recommend that: (1) this draft be revised in a negotiation process involving several sectors of the University community (administrators, staC, faculty, student organizations).
The revision should seek a balance between the administration’s control needs and recognition of the University’s special role in society as a place where dissent is protected; (2) minor, symbolic, and incidental acts be removed from the list of chargeable oCences; and (3) exceptions to the rules laid down be granted either in writing or verbally.

Thomas Zorabedian, Ed.D.
Adjunct Professor, Film/Media and Honors Program Former Assistant Dean, URI College of Arts & Sciences zman@uri.edu RE: Proposed “Regulations Regarding Use of University Property” At its best, a university is a marketplace of ideas.
These ideas may be, and often are, diverse and contradictory, or even at times contentious.
At its weakest, universities discourage or even squelch the free exchange of opinions, beliefs, and feelings.
I recall a time, including specifically at URI, when students and faculty regularly embraced the former approach and engaged in lively interactions.
I fear that the trend in general seems to be in a different direction of less tolerance for public and disparate engagement on campus.
To this end, parts of the proposed regulations raise some concerns that they are not entirely in keeping with the university’s mission which specifically refers to “the freedom to learn” and the “dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.” Most of the regulations regarding the “control and use” of the university property seem reasonable, sensible, and even innocuous.

Of course, I agree that the destruction, defacing, and vandalizing of property and violation of various laws should be prohibited.
However, two sections include language that could unnecessarily restrict the freedom of expression, and in fact could discourage or even severely punish those who choose to express and share their ideas: 2(f): “Leafletting and Distribution of Literature.” The proposal only allows this time-tested approach “provided that the activity does not impede the flow of pedestrian or vehicular traffic…or create litter.” What exactly does this mean?
Is this a major problem?
While no one should force material on anyone, does going up to someone while they are walking and stopping to give them material “impede” them?
And, if someone who is given some material throws it away, is the person handing it out in violation of littering?
These are not irrelevant questions, because section 3 refers to “suspension or expulsion” as a possible enforcement, a draconian response. 2(g): “Signs, Posters, Banners.” Again, signs that create permanent or temporary damage should not be allowed.

But, could students who attach a sign or drape a banner to a wall, dorm balcony, or building be suspended or expelled, as per section 3?
URI has had innumerable instances over the years of students displaying sentiments or slogans, with the intent of “contributing to the public good,” with no damage to university property.
In fact, the lack of such signage has been conspicuous over the last decade or so.
Further, this section states that “no signs supported by standards or sticks shall be permitted in any assembly inside any building.” If this were a regulation at our country’s national conventions, a good percentage of the attendees would have been thrown out or arrested.
I assume the concern is that a “stick” may become a weapon of some kind.
Obviously, that kind of usage should not be tolerated and should be dealt with harshly.
However, because signs and banners are often held up by some means of support, it follows that the peaceful use of this method of expression should be allowed.
Further, it would be refreshing to see more of this on a campus when students usually seem uninvolved in political, cultural, or social issues.

While I understand that damage to university property can be costly, time-consuming, and aesthetically disagreeable, one of the great and important traditions and freedoms of university life, including at URI, since the late 1960s has been the thoughtful sharing and display of ideas and information.
We should do what we can to encourage that essential aspect of learning, rather than develop new ways to suppress it.
Respectfully submitted, Thomas Zorabedian

Theodore Walls, Faculty Senate President URI Faculty Senate Executive Committee Dear Ted: Per the request of FSEC to provide comments on a proposed University Regulation under consideration by the Senate and the wider URI community, I offer the following observations.
In Section 2 of the proposed regulation there is a listing of Limitations and Prohibited Activities.
In many of these prohibited practices, there is a tacit disregard for the tools by which those with less power within established social hierarchies can express their point of view with enough impact to effectively communicate with powerful decision makers.
As Frederick Douglas once wrote, “Power concedes nothing without a demand.
It never did and it never will.” The University of Rhode Island largely since the Presidency of Francis Horn in the 1960s has strongly embraced a principles of community free speech in opposition of national public policies such as the Vietnam War, and in the late 1970s in response to unfair state labor practices.
Notably, the former provost Beverly Swan (of Swan Hall fame) was a prominent protester staffing the luncheon buffets set up during the high-profile faculty strike.

Moreover, there has been effective protest of university policies that have led to meaningful positive changes at URI.
In the early 1990s, effective protests by the “Brothers United” occupied Taft Hall over civil rights issues and greater emphasis on racial equity at URI.
There was effective communication to President Carothers and the RI Board of Governors for Higher Education that something was very wrong at URI in race relations.
President Carothers then went on to establish the Multicultural Center in the center of campus.
It seems reasonable to prohibit violence or endangerment to others by university regulation, but some other proposed regulations may constitute only a minor nuisance to community members.
These proposed regulations include disruption of meetings, impeding building entry for a while, etc. might be tolerated for a time and resolved by official dialog.
Various other practices listed for possible prohibition could be construed as ordinary vigorous expressions of free speech, including leafleting, signs, posters, banners, erection of structures, camping overnight as part of protest action although a nuisance.
Nuisance is the point!

Why would protesters go through the bother unless they felt something important to say?
Picking up after protesters is not much different than cleaning up after a football game.
The one of the most egregious “Catch 22s” of the proposed regulation is in item o, “Sanitation.
Outdoors” in which defecation or urination is prohibited.
This seems reasonable at first glance, but this item is accompanied by item k, Building Access, where all the restrooms are located.
One might avail of a sanitation company to bring in temporary latrines to service protesters, but this

might be construed as violating item i “Erection of Structures”, requiring permission of the VP. What if the VP is not sympathetic to the cause of the protesters and denies permission to protest? Could the bodily functions be used as a weapon against sustained free speech activities? One of the most prominent non-sequiturs in the proposed regulations is item m, prohibiting bicycles, skateboards and other conveyances on campus. In an era of developing alternatives to fossil fuels, any sort of carbon-free transport to the university from outside and within the university should be encouraged rather than discouraged. Perhaps a joint senate and administration effort to develop vehicular traffic norms around campus may be a more effective strategy of maintaining pedestrian safety. Thank you for this opportunity to comment. Sincerely, Michael A. Rice, PhD Faculty Senator, CELS

COMMENTS ON PROPOSED UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES REGULATIONS REGARDING USE OF UNIVERSITY PROPERTY October 2024 The American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island appreciates the opportunity to offer comments on the Board of Trustees’ proposed regulations regarding University Property . We understand that they are designed to convey the University of Rhode Island’s commitment to quality education through the use and protection of its University Property. Some provisions in these proposed regulations, however, also have a deleterious effect, even if unintentional, on the University’s concomitant commitment to protecting academic freedom and the First Amendment rights of students. It is with the goal of safeguarding those rights that we offer the following comments for consideration. The Proposed Regulations 1. Section 2(a). Individual Rights: This section prevents using University Property “in a manner that impinges upon the rights of another person under the United States or Rhode Island Constitution; any federal, state, or local law; or any University policy.” While one cannot argue with this goal in the abstract, we are concerned about its potential misuse in implementation. On university campuses across the country, we have recently seen conflicts where student speech on political matters is said – often unfairly, in our view – to impinge on the rights of other students to feel safe or free from discrimination. Section 2(e).
Endangerment: This section prohibits the use of University Property to “endanger” others.
The word “endanger” is undefined, which leaves it open to wide interpretation and, again, potentially applicable to protected speech.
We would urge that the wording be clarified to explicitly refer to physical endangerment. 3.
Section 2(f).
Leafletting and Distribution of Literature: This section would allow the university to bar leafletting or distribution of literature if it “create[s] litter.” This is extremely problematic and should be stricken.
The exercise of free speech rights cannot be prohibited because of the improper behavior of others.
Littering by students who receive a leaflet is out of the control of the distributor, yet this provision would allow for the denial of the leafleteer’s First Amendment rights on the basis of a third party’s actions.
For close to a century, the U.S.

Supreme Court has rejected such efforts.1 Also, while leafletters should not be allowed to block access to buildings or walkways while engaged in this quintessential First Amendment activity, we are concerned that the rule’s ban on “impeding” the flow of pedestrian traffic could be interpreted in an overly restrictive manner.
After all, any distribution of literature has the potential to contribute to temporary bottlenecks, but that should not serve as a basis for prohibiting it. 1 As far back as 1939, the Court noted: “We are of opinion that the purpose to keep the streets clean and of good appearance is insu=icient to justify an ordinance which prohibits a person rightfully on a public street from handing literature to one willing to receive it. . . .
There are obvious methods of preventing littering.
Amongst these is the punishment of those who actually throw papers on the streets.” Schneider v.
State, 308 U.S. 147, 162 (1939).
